notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for **1 Kings 20:23–43**, drawing from the sources I was able to reach. (My search and fetch limits were reached, so I could not retrieve dedicated pages from Reformed, Catholic, Orthodox, or modern scholarly sites. Where those are absent, I have noted it.)

---

## v. 23 — The Syrians’ Flawed Theology

The servants of Ben-hadad, anxious to explain their defeat, attribute it not to their own drunken negligence nor to Israelite valor, but to the gods of Israel being “gods of the hills.” In ancient polytheism, deities were thought to have localized authority—some over mountains, others over rivers, woods, or valleys. Since Samaria and the recent battle lay in the hill-country of Ephraim, the Syrians concluded that Israel’s God held power only there and would be powerless on the plains. This was a common pagan notion of “tutelary” or territorial gods. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/20-23.htm — Ellicott)

Gill notes that the Syrians may have derived this idea from reports of God giving the Law on Mount Sinai, the recent miracle on Mount Carmel, and Israel’s custom of worshiping on “high places.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/20-23.htm — Gill)

The Pulpit Commentary adds that the advice was probably not purely religious: underneath the superstition was a shrewd military calculation—chariots and cavalry, Syria’s strength, could be deployed far more effectively on level ground. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/20-23.htm — Pulpit)

David Guzik (Enduring Word, charismatic/Pentecostal tradition) quotes Spurgeon at length: “The art of god-making is very common among men. Instead of going to revelation to see what God is… men sit down and consider what sort of God he ought to be.” Spurgeon also applied this to the church of his own day: “Is he the God of the hills of persecution, but not the God of the valleys of prosperity?” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/)

---

## v. 24 — Dismiss the Vassal Kings

Ben-hadad’s servants also advise him to remove the thirty-two tributary kings and replace them with his own appointed officers (*captains* or *governors*). Gill explains that these kings were likely unused to war and given to pleasure; they would not fight with the commitment of professional soldiers loyal directly to Ben-hadad. It was also a move to centralize military command. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-20.html — Gill)

Keil & Delitzsch concur: the vassal-kings had probably “not shown the desired self-sacrifice for the cause of their superior” in the first campaign. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/20-23.htm — Keil & Delitzsch)

---

## v. 25 — Raise an Equal Army; Fight on the Plain

The Syrians propose to rebuild their army to its former strength—horse for horse, chariot for chariot—and fight Israel on the plain, confident they will prevail. The advice is coherent within their theology: move the battle to terrain where (they think) Israel’s God has no jurisdiction and where Syrian chariotry has the advantage. Ben-hadad approves and acts accordingly. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/)

---

## v. 26 — Ben-hadad Marches to Aphek

In the spring (the season when ancient Near Eastern kings typically went to war, cf. 2 Samuel 11:1), Ben-hadad musters the Arameans and goes up to Aphek to fight Israel. Aphek means “fortress” and there are several places bearing that name. Ellicott identifies two likely candidates: one in the plain of Esdraelon, the other about six miles east of the Sea of Galilee on the road to Damascus. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-20.html — Ellicott)

---

## v. 27 — Israel’s Tiny Army

Israel also mobilizes, gathers supplies, and marches out. But the contrast is stark: Israel encamped “like two little flocks of goats” while the Arameans “covered the countryside.” Guzik notes that Ben-hadad came with overwhelming force, determined not to risk another humiliation. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/) Ellicott observes that the relatively small Israelite numbers, even after the previous year’s great victory, suggest Ahab had suffered earlier defeats that had broken Israel’s military strength. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-20.html)

---

## v. 28 — The Man of God’s Promise: “You Shall Know that I Am the LORD”

A “man of God” (likely a different unnamed prophet from the one in v. 13, per Ellicott) approaches the king of Israel. The LORD’s stated reason for granting victory is explicit: because the Arameans have said “the LORD is a god of the hills and not of the valleys,” God will deliver the great army into Israel’s hand so that they—and the Syrians—will know that He is the LORD. Guzik stresses that God took the flawed theology of the Syrians “as a personal insult.” Our wrong ideas about God always detract from His glory. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/)

Ellicott adds that this vindication of God’s majesty before foreign nations echoes Solomon’s prayer and the Psalms—a foreshadowing of the prophetic theme that all nations are in some sense accountable to know the one true God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-20.html)

---

## vv. 29–30 — The Seven-Day Standoff and Massive Defeat

The armies camp opposite each other for seven days. On the seventh day, battle is joined, and Israel strikes down 100,000 Aramean foot soldiers in a single day. The survivors flee into the walled city of Aphek, where the wall collapses on 27,000 of the remaining men. Ben-hadad hides in an inner chamber of the city. Guzik calls the 100,000 a “clear miracle,” yet one that worked through the existing army, not an outside agency. The collapsing wall was a further extraordinary divine intervention. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/) Ellicott notes that the numbers are very large and raises the possibility of textual corruption, though the same numbers appear in the ancient versions; he also points out that massed Oriental armies in confined spaces produced staggering slaughter-rates in ancient warfare. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-20.html)

---

## v. 31 — Sackcloth and Ropes

Ben-hadad’s servants now advise a posture of extreme self-abasement: sackcloth on the waist and ropes around the head. This was the gesture of captives offering themselves as naked, helpless criminals to sue for mercy. They have heard that “the kings of the house of Israel are merciful kings.” Guzik notes the irony: not long before, Ben-hadad had pronounced severe threats against Ahab; now he humbles himself as completely as possible. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/) Ellicott compares the ropes to “the ropes round the necks of the burghers of Calais” in the days of Edward III. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-20.html)

---

## v. 32 — “Your Servant Ben-hadad… Please Spare My Life”

The envoys approach Ahab with the message: “Your servant Ben-hadad says, ‘Please spare my life.’” Ahab’s response, “Is he still alive? He is my brother,” is striking. The English Puritan John Trapp remarks: “This was not courtesy, but foolery. Brother Ben-hadad will ere long fight against Ahab with that life which he had given him.” (Quoted in https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/)

---

## v. 33 — The Men Grasp at the Sign of Hope

The Syrian envoys are watching closely for any “sign of hope” (literally, the LXX says “as for augury”). When Ahab says “my brother,” they quickly seize on the word and reply, “Yes, your brother Ben-hadad.” In Eastern custom, the term “brother” implied a pledge of amity not to be revoked. Ahab then says, “Go and get him!” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-20.html — Ellicott)

---

## v. 34 — A Treaty and Release

Ben-hadad comes out, and Ahab invites him up into his own chariot—a public act sealing their new relationship (cf. 2 Kings 10:15–16). Ben-hadad offers to restore the cities his father took from Ahab’s father and to grant Ahab trading quarters (“marketplaces” / “streets”) in Damascus, just as Ben-hadad’s father had set up in Samaria. Ahab replies, “By this treaty I release you,” makes a covenant with him, and sends him away. 

Guzik is blunt: “Ahab had no business making this treaty. The victory was the LORD’s and did not belong to Ahab; he had no right to negotiate away the victory.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/) F. B. Meyer calls Ahab’s easy good-nature “criminal” and says that the judge may feel compassion but must be governed by the good of all; Ahab’s “unwise clemency” later brought suffering on Israel at the hand of Syria. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/1-kings-20.html)

---

## v. 35 — “Strike Me, Please”

A certain man “of the sons of the prophets” (the first explicit mention of this phrase in Scripture) tells his companion by the word of the LORD to strike him. The companion refuses. Ellicott notes that “sons of the prophets” means discipleship, not hereditary succession; these were likely communities or schools of prophetic training revived after the victory over Baal-worship at Carmel. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-20.html)

Josephus (Antiquities 8.14.5) identifies this unnamed prophet with Micaiah son of Imlah, who figures prominently in 1 Kings 22—a tradition or conjecture that fits the subsequent narrative. (Cited in https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/ and Ellicott)

---

## v. 36 — The Lion’s Judgment

Because the companion refused to obey the voice of the LORD, the prophet declares that a lion will kill him as soon as he departs—and it happens. Adam Clarke explains the severity: “This person was also one of the sons of the prophets, and he knew that God frequently delivered his counsels in this way, and should have immediately obeyed; for the smiting could have had no evil in it when God commanded it.” (Quoted in https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/) Ellicott compares the parallel in 1 Kings 13:24, where another disobedient prophet is killed by a lion. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-20.html)

---

## vv. 37–38 — The Wound and the Disguise

The prophet finds a second man, who obeys and strikes him, inflicting a wound. Then the prophet waits by the road, disguising himself with a bandage over his eyes (the BSB says “bandage over his eyes”; KJV/older translations have “ashes upon his face”). Guzik explains that Ahab “consciously shielded himself from the prophets,” which is why the disguise was necessary. The wound serves to make the prophet look like a soldier returning from battle, lending credibility to his parable. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/) Ellicott notes that unless the wound had symbolic significance (applied to Ahab or Israel), it is difficult to see what purpose it served beyond the disguise. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-20.html)

---

## vv. 39–40 — The Parable of the Escaped Prisoner

As the king passes, the disguised prophet cries out with a story: he was in the midst of battle when a man entrusted him with guarding a captive, on pain of his own life or a talent of silver (about 75 pounds / 34 kg of silver—a vast sum). “While your servant was busy here and there, the man disappeared.” 

Ahab immediately pronounces judgment: “So shall your judgment be; you have pronounced it on yourself.” The king has condemned himself. Guzik notes the application: the excuse “busy here and there” was no excuse at all; “he should have paid attention to the job he had to do.” Spurgeon applied this to lost spiritual opportunities: “Time past is gone. You can never have it back again.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/) Bell’s Baptist Commentary draws the same lesson: “be careful about being busy with so many petty details, we may end up missing divinely given opportunities.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cbb/1-kings-20.html)

---

## v. 41 — The Prophet Revealed

The prophet quickly removes the bandage, and Ahab recognizes him as one of the prophets. Keil & Delitzsch remark that this revelation showed Ahab clearly that the whole story was a parable designed to trap him. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/20-42.htm — Keil & Delitzsch)

---

## v. 42 — The Sentence: Life for Life, People for People

The prophet delivers the word of the LORD: “Because you have let slip from your hand the man I had devoted to destruction (*ḥerem* — under the ban, devoted, cursed), your life will be exchanged for his life, and your people for his people.”

**The nature of Ahab’s sin:** Commentators across traditions agree that this parallels Saul’s disobedience in sparing Agag (1 Samuel 15). Matthew Poole asks what Ahab’s great sin was and answers: the dishonor done to God by letting a blasphemer go unpunished contrary to Leviticus 24:16; God had delivered Ben-hadad into Ahab’s hand precisely because of that blasphemy (v. 28). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/20-42.htm — Poole) The Pulpit Commentary expands: Ahab was not free to do as he liked; the victories were God’s, the war was God’s war, and he should have consulted a prophet before disposing of the prisoners. Ahab “arrogated to himself their fruits, and thereby ignored and dishonoured God.” Moreover, he defied all Old Testament precedents (Joshua 10:26; Judges 7:25; 1 Samuel 15:33). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/20-42.htm — Pulpit)

Ellicott adds that even “soft-heartedness, as in the case of Eli, may be treason to the cause of righteousness.” The prophet speaks “partly as a patriot, jealous… of the lenity which left the deadly enemy of Israel unsubdued.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/20-42.htm — Ellicott)

**The term “devoted to destruction” (*ḥerem*):** Barnes and Cambridge note that the Hebrew literally reads “the man of my ban” or “the man of my curse”—one laid under the *ḥerem*, which in Leviticus 27:29 required the devoted thing to be put to death. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/20-42.htm — Barnes; Cambridge)

**Fulfillment:** Gill, Benson, and Poole all note that “your life shall go for his life” was fulfilled when Ahab died by a Syrian arrow at Ramoth-gilead (1 Kings 22:34). “Your people for his people” was fulfilled later under Hazael, who devastated Israel (2 Kings 8:12; 10:32–33). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/20-42.htm — Gill; Benson)

G. Campbell Morgan (a Congregationalist/evangelical expositor) comments: “Pity which produces disobedience to the divine command is sin.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gcm/1-kings-20.html) Coffman likewise: “God delivered Benhadad into Ahab’s hand in order that Ahab might execute him.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/1-kings-20.html)

---

## v. 43 — Sullen and Angry

Ahab went home to Samaria “sullen and angry” (BSB; KJV “heavy and displeased”). The Hebrew words (*sar wə-zāʿēp̄*) convey being stubborn, fretful, and resentful—the same language used of Ahab sulking over Naboth’s vineyard in 1 Kings 21:4. 

Lange, quoted in the Pulpit Homiletics, observes: “There is no help for the man who allows himself to be irritated by the truth instead of receiving it with meekness (James 1:21).” (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/20-43.html) Trapp says Ahab’s heavy displeasure was “not with a sorrow according to God, but such as arose from a slavish fear.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/20-43.html — Trapp)

Guzik summarizes: “Ahab was sullen and displeased, but he was not repentant. He had the sorrow of the world that brings death, not the sorrow of godly repentance.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/)

Matthew Henry echoes: “Ahab went to his house, heavy and displeased, not truly penitent, or seeking to undo what he had done amiss; every way out of humour, notwithstanding his victory.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/20-42.htm — Matthew Henry)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

The sources I was able to retrieve do not show sharp *denominational* disagreement on this passage. The traditional reading is broadly shared across evangelical, Reformed, Baptist, and Pentecostal/charismatic lines:

- **Reformed / Presbyterian:** No specific Reformed-source page was retrieved (searches to ligonier.org, monergism.org, thegospelcoalition.org returned no usable results for this passage). The commentaries from Gill (a Baptist but widely read by Reformed), Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran/Reformed), and the Pulpit Commentary (broadly Reformed Anglican) are consistent with the mainstream interpretation.
- **Baptist:** Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary draws the application toward lost opportunities and warns believers not to be “too busy to do what the Lord has for one to do.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-kings-20.html) Spurgeon (Baptist), quoted extensively by Guzik, applied the “god of the hills but not the valleys” idea to the church in different eras—persecution versus prosperity. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/)
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic:** Enduring Word (David Guzik, associated with Calvary Chapel) offers the fullest verse-by-verse treatment and aligns closely with the traditional evangelical reading, with a strong emphasis on God’s power working through unlikely instruments and the application of “busy here and there” as a warning about spiritual distraction. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/)
- **Methodist/Wesleyan:** No results were retrieved from seedbed.com or wesley.nnu.edu. Matthew Henry (nonconformist, widely used by Methodists) gives a concise, application-heavy reading. Benson Commentary (Methodist-leaning Anglican) stresses the dishonor to God in sparing a blasphemer and traces the fulfillment of the judgment. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/20-42.htm — Benson)
- **Lutheran:** No pages from lcms.org or 1517.org were retrieved. Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran) provides philological and theological notes consistent with the general interpretation. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/20-23.htm)

---

## Other Views

**Catholic and Orthodox:** No pages were retrieved from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org for this passage. The Catholic Haydock Commentary is listed on biblehub.com but its text was not fetched.

**Modern Scholarship:** No results were found from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org. The Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges (moderately critical) notes that the Syrians likely used the singular “their god is a god of the hills” (RV), reflecting a national-deity concept, and acknowledges that the large casualty numbers may reflect textual issues. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/20-23.htm — Cambridge)

**Popular / Debated Modern Teachings:** No results were retrieved addressing prosperity, Word of Faith, or hyper-grace readings of this passage. The text’s emphasis on God’s sovereignty over all terrain (hills *and* valleys) is occasionally used in charismatic contexts to teach that God’s power is not limited to certain circumstances, but no explicitly prosperity-gospel interpretation was found in the searched sources.
